segments.text: A Sociocognitive Structural-Flow Framework for Explainable Pre-Assault Prediction through Micro-Action Algebra and Counterfactual Intent Simulation Abstract- We introduce SENTINEL, a novel neuro-symbolic sociocognitive framework for interpretable pre-assault prediction in dynamic and multi-agent worlds. In contrast to these conventional deep learning methods that learn superficial correlations, which serve as a building block of the atomic behavior model for action composition, SENTINEL applies MAA to encode fine-grained behavior micro-atoms and STF modeling to uncover causal influences among temporal micro-action sequences. The RHSE unit is able to effectively model the collective interactions among multiple subjects and can well address crowded parts or partial occlusions. Additionally, the transparency is enhanced with the Counterfactual Intent Simulator (CIS) which creates counterfactual “what-if” scenarios and explains "why" a decision was made and establishes operator trust: interpretability. The system is based on a survival-guided Early-Time Risk Calibration Loss, while preserving probability consistency of threat estimation. Experiments on benchmark datasets like RWF-2000, XD-Violence and the proposed PreAssault-CHI present strong performance gains with 96.84%, early prediction accuracy, 94.31% causal edge precision rate and 92.75% counterfactual explanation fidelity. In addition, the model achieves a 93.12% fairness parity among demographic subgroups and achieves a 38% decrease in false-positive alarms compared to previous RNN-based and transformer-based baselinesี่. These results highlight SENTINEL’s ability to provide timely, interpretable, and ethically aligned early-warning signals for security-critical environments, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and cognitive transparency in human-AI decision collaboration. Keywords- Pre-assault prediction, micro-action algebra, structural temporal flow, relational hypergraph, counterfactual reasoning, early warning, explainable AI, causal modeling, multi-agent interaction, calibrated risk prediction, ethical surveillance, human-AI collaboration. I Introduction Anticipating violent behavior in advance is a challenging problem and interesting to a variety of domains including human-robot interaction, surveillance, behavioral science, and human-AI fusion [1],[2]. Earlier research on anticipation of early action has demonstrated that preparatory cues—minimal body movements, changes in gaze direction, oscillographic micro‐actions—convey information about intent substantially before actual aggression [3],[4]. This in turn has led to the development of a catalogue of known pre-attack (pre-assault) behavioral and physiological indicators including posture, tension in limbs, altered breathing or facial expression, body orientation toward others [5],[6], scanning behaviors (e.g. looking for threats) defensive displays and verbal cues. Ethical considerations also complicate the use of “black-box” predictors: trust is lost when operators or those affected cannot explain why a prediction has been made, especially with respect to demographic or social variation [8], [9]. The additional obstruction caused by human presence in a crowded or partly occluded environment creates even more challenges. The effects of these conditions—there being audience or no audience, limbs and interruptions from the environment—are too obscure the micro-actions and situational changes in their world. And social interaction models which consider the structural relations between multiple agents also show promising results, such as hypergraph representations and relational encoders by learning interactions among all different agents besides pair wise or scene representation baselines [10], [11].If you do not model the interaction graphs, you face the challenge of signal mixing or context collapse- i.e., micro-acts of one agent are mixed with those of others or buried social signals may coexist. The temporal flow of actions—an ordered sequence of preparatory behaviors—necessitates modeling not merely the correlation between events, but their causal antecedence, so as to justify interventions or alarms based on more than an increase in accuracy alone, accordingly making sense of how risk develops [12],[13]. Another gap in existing literature is lack of counterfactual reasoning: knowing that an assault is predicted is insufficient unless one can examine “what if” alternatives, showing how changes in behavior or context would alter outcome [14],[15]. Counterfactual models have been used in other domains (e.g. healthcare, safety) to increase transparency, but seldom in pre-assault risk prediction. Also, calibration of early risk: high stakes environments require high sensitivity to early signs without overwhelming false positives [16],[17]. Loss functions that discount late recognition or that encourage early detection while maintaining probabilistic consistency are needed but under-explored. Finally, fairness across demographic subgroups—across gender, ethnicity, age, body type—must be measured, since many visual/behavioral models exhibit bias [18],[19],[20]. This research proposes a framework that addresses all the above: atomization of micro-actions with algebraic structure, explicit temporal causal flow, relational encoding of multiple agents, counterfactual explanation modules, early-time risk calibration, and fairness assessment. Extensive experiments on datasets including RWF-2000, XD-Violence, and a newly collected PreAssault-CHI dataset allow evaluation of early prediction accuracy, causal structure precision, and explanation fidelity. The results show strong performance under each measure, lower false positives, and the robustness of parity across racial groups. The paper is characterized by the following innovative contributions: ●​ Formalization of Micro-Action Algebra (MAA) and Structural Temporal Flow (STF) modules, capturing the minimal behavioural atoms and its connected causal effect to support intelligible chaining of micro-actions within pre-assault chains. ●​ Relational Hypergraph Social Context Encoder (RHSE) combined with a Counterfactual Intent Simulator (CIS) to obtain scenario-level explanations (“what if

The MAA discretizes human motion into a set of atoms of behaviors to allow the algebraic manipulation with micro-actions and represent illations about intentions over time [21]. At the same time, RHSE module encodes collective interactions in a multi-agent environment by relational hypergraphs, enabling the model to learn grouplevel dynamics and social context dependencies [24]. For interpretability, a Counterfactual Intent Simulator (CIS) generates counterfactual paths and offers “what-if” explanations on why the model made a decision in human cognitive-friendly style [25]. Experiments on RWF-2000, XD-Violence and the proposed PreAssault-CHI dataset show that SENTINEL achieves 96.84% early prediction accuracy (EPA), 94.31% causal edge precision (CEP), 92.75% counterfactual explanation fidelity (CEF), and fairness parity 93.12%, with a false alarm reduction by 38% compared to recurrent and transformer based baselines. Extensive ablation studies validate the distinct effects of STF, CIS and MAA on predictive accuracy, causal reasoning and explainability respectively, demonstrating the synergy of our framework design. SENTINEL is capable of encoding fine-grained behavioral atoms, reasoning over temporal causal flows and simulating “what-if” scenarios making early-warning prediction both timely and interpretable. In addition, by incorporating RHSE, the proposed formulation adaptively responds in congested and partly occluded multi-agent cases, while the survival-based early-time risk calibration facilitates reliable probabilistic threat assessment. Qualitative analysis demonstrates that micro-action histories and counterfactual explanations are consistent, interpretable and actionable, necessary for human-AI collaboration in
